timeline.summary: Mikey reviews appearance-centered pickup theories and states that appearance attracts initial attention while behavior matters more for sustained attraction.
He constructs an evolutionary 'hunter traits' model involving body shape, movement, eye contact, pace, confidence and decisiveness.
He claims women need longer to assess safety and consistency, then links emotional stability to survival cues and modern social conditioning to loss of self.
Modern status ideals, subcultures and named celebrity relationships are used to argue that behavior can outweigh conventional looks and status.
He distinguishes attention from attraction, introduces social proof as a shortcut, and says looks and behavioral traits can coexist independently.
He attributes confidence differences partly to childhood appearance feedback, encouragement, jealousy or bullying, including his own acne and bullying story.
He closes by calling looks a basic threshold and urging viewers to develop confidence and individual behavioral expression.
The remaining ASR is multilingual noise and an overlong final segment; it is excluded from semantic claims and clamped to media duration.

examples.summary: Pan-Lü-Deng-Xiao-Xian, peacock signaling and popular pickup books are reviewed as prior models before Mikey rejects appearance as decisive.
Named celebrities and subcultures are used as anecdotes for behavior overriding conventional looks or status; the relationship claims are not independently verified.

visual_findings: All 21 sampled frames were reviewed. The host appears throughout an edited essay intercut with Titanic, DNA imagery, predators, period film scenes, celebrity/public clips and a crowd event.
The visuals illustrate the narration but show no study, dataset or traceable primary source for the evolutionary, gender or attraction claims.
No chat screenshot or second live participant appears in the sparse sample; no dense visual window was required for the narration-level distillation.

permissions.reason: Potentially useful distinctions about appearance, attention and behavior are intertwined with pseudoscience, gender stereotypes, named allegations and an ASR duration error.

limitations: Media duration is 967.25 seconds, while the final ASR segment ends at 972.90 seconds; no evidence is cited beyond media duration and the noisy tail is excluded.
Automatic transcript was not checked word-for-word against original audio.
Twenty-one sparse frames do not equal continuous audio-visual verification.
Evolutionary, developmental and gender claims are uncited and cannot be treated as scientific findings.
